Format JSON without rounding large numbers

Format or minify JSON while retaining large-number digits, decimal notation, string escapes and duplicate keys. Check syntax, limits and downstream risks.

Start with the original JSON text

Paste the original response or file text into JSON formatter. Choose Format JSON for indented output or Minify for compact output. Both operations preserve tokens while changing whitespace outside strings. Keep an original copy and compare important fields before copying or downloading the result. Toolnest processes this input in your browser without an account.

Why a parse-and-save workflow can change digits

JavaScript number conversion can lose precision. A formatter that parses a value and then serializes the parsed object can therefore change a large numeric identifier. Toolnest uses parsing only to check syntax; its output comes from the original text tokens. The example 9007199254740993123 remains those exact digits. This is text preservation, not arbitrary-precision arithmetic or a promise about the next application.

Keep strings and numeric notation intact

Minifying must not remove spaces inside quoted strings. For example, the space in "a b" belong to the value. Toolnest also retains escape spelling, decimal notation such as 1.00, exponent notation such as -2.50E+3 and negative-zero spelling. It does not normalize these values. If an identifier is already damaged, return to its source; do not guess replacement digits.

Review duplicate keys before using the data

A token-preserving formatter retains both members in an object such as {"same":1,"same":2}. That avoids silently deleting source text during formatting, but it does not settle which value your application should use. RFC 8259 recommends unique object names because receivers handle duplicates differently. Resolve the conflict upstream. Toolnest does not detect or warn about every duplicate key, and a successful syntax check is not a duplicate-key audit.

Fix syntax deliberately

Standard JSON uses double quotes for strings and property names. It does not accept comments, trailing commas, NaN or Infinity. The formatter displays a parser error and clears its output for invalid syntax. Read the reported location and compare the surrounding source. Do not remove punctuation or quote numeric fields merely to silence an error; those edits can change the data’s meaning or its compatibility with an API.

Check the receiving system as well

A valid JSON document can still violate a schema or exceed an application’s numeric range. For example, the token 1e400 can be preserved as text even though a receiver using ordinary JavaScript numbers cannot represent its finite mathematical value. If you control the data contract, consider string identifiers or a suitable precise-number representation. Agree the representation with the receiver instead of changing a number to a string without checking its schema.

Stay within the browser tool limits

Input is limited to 2,097,152 UTF-8 bytes. Indented output is capped at 8,388,608 JavaScript string code units and 100 nesting levels. Minify can handle deeper syntactically valid input within the input-size limit, but is still subject to browser resources. These are tool limits, not universal JSON limits. Split large work at valid document boundaries or use a suitable local workflow when this browser tool is insufficient.

Download and verify the result

Use Download JSON after successful formatting or minification. Check that the intended source document was used, especially after handling an invalid input. Formatting does not redact personal data, validate an API schema, sign a request or produce canonical JSON for hashing. Keep authentication tokens and other secrets out of shared screenshots and examples.

Common questions

Will formatting round my large JSON numbers?

Toolnest validates syntax with JSON.parse, then formats the original tokens instead of serializing the parsed values. The numeric text is retained. Receiving software can still round it when it parses the output.

Can the formatter recover an identifier that was already rounded?

No. Start with the original JSON text. If another application already changed the digits, formatting cannot infer the missing value. A quoted identifier is a different data type; use strings only when the receiving schema allows them.

Are duplicate JSON keys safe to use?

Object names should be unique for reliable interchange. Toolnest retains repeated members without resolving them. A different parser may keep only one value or reject the object. Resolve the conflict in the source data before relying on it.

Does Valid JSON mean my API request is correct?

No. Syntax validation does not check required fields, allowed values, types, business rules or the receiving application’s numeric limits. Test against the API’s documented schema separately.

Can I format JSON comments or trailing commas?

No. This tool expects standard JSON. Comments, trailing commas, single-quoted strings, NaN and Infinity are rejected. Correct the source intentionally rather than assuming a formatter can safely repair it.

Sources and further reading

  • RFC 8259: JSON grammar, object names and numeric interoperability
